look: Marble temples and halls around the Forum, and brick apartment blocks called insulae, up to five or six floors high, with red tile roofs. The Colosseum was nearly finished: it opened in AD 80.
Men wore a knee-length tunic with a belt. Citizens put on the heavy white toga for public business. Women wore a long dress called a stola with a shawl, the palla, over it.
Mostly on foot. A law from Julius Caesar's time kept most carts off the streets by day, so deliveries rumbled through at night. The rich were carried in litters.
No street lamps. People carried oil lamps or torches, and slaves with torches walked ahead of the rich.
In AD 79 the emperor Vespasian died and his son Titus took over. That year Mount Vesuvius buried Pompeii, near Naples, and that is why its paintings survived.

stops.name: In a Roman forum (a painting from Pompeii)
stops.made: Painted on a wall in Pompeii, before AD 79
stops.title: Scenes of the forum, from the estate of Julia Felix
stops.note: Nobody photographed Rome in the Caesars' time, so this walk uses what Romans painted and what survived. This real Roman wall painting comes from Pompeii, a Roman town near Naples.

spots.d: Forums were lined with columns holding up a roof, so people could shop and talk out of the sun and rain.
spots.how: Painted columns divide this whole painting, and the real columns still stand in Pompeii's forum.

spots.d: Most people wore a simple tunic to the knee, with a cloak over it when it was cool.
spots.how: Roman paintings and statues show the same clothes again and again.

spots.d: Children came to the forum with their parents. Some boys had lessons there too, with a teacher in the open air.
spots.how: Another part of this same painting shows a school lesson in the forum.

stops.name: The Roman Forum, looking to the Capitol
stops.title: The Forum Romanum against the Capitol
stops.note: Taken about 1,800 years later. The ruins show where the Forum of AD 79 stood.

spots.t: Roman walls under a later palace
spots.d: The lower stone walls are the Tabularium, Rome's records office, built in 78 BC. In AD 79 it was already 150 years old.
spots.how: Medieval and Renaissance Romans built the city hall on top of it, and it is still there.

spots.d: The tower and palace on top were built in the Middle Ages and the 1500s, so they were not here in AD 79.
spots.how: They are Rome's city hall today.

spots.d: This arch was built in AD 203 for the emperor Septimius Severus, more than a hundred years after 79.
spots.how: Its inscription names the emperor and his sons.

spots.d: By 1860 the Forum was half buried, and Romans called it the Campo Vaccino, the Cow Field, because cattle grazed there.
spots.how: Proper digging of the Forum only got going later in the 1800s.

spots.d: Rome kept its state treasury in this temple. A temple stood here in AD 79, though these columns come from a rebuilding in the 300s.
spots.how: Its eight columns still stand in the Forum.

spots.d: In AD 79 the Colosseum was a building site. Titus opened it in AD 80 with 100 days of games.
spots.how: Roman writers describe the opening games.

spots.d: Big stones of the Forum's streets, worn by carts and feet.
spots.how: Stones like these still lie in the Forum today.

stops.name: Inside a Roman house, in Pompeii
stops.title: Painted walls in the estate of Julia Felix, Pompeii
stops.note: The walls were painted by Romans; the photograph is modern.

spots.d: Romans loved strong red, yellow and black walls. Reds came from minerals such as red ochre.
spots.how: The paint survived under the volcanic ash of AD 79.

spots.d: A niche for a lamp, a statue or the small gods that guarded the household.
spots.how: Many houses in Pompeii have niches like this.

spots.d: Panels painted to look like framed pictures and columns, to make a small room feel grand.
spots.how: Pompeii's houses are full of painted architecture like this.
